strengths: Clearly motivated and practically useful problem formulation: enabling target-aware actor-object interaction in image-to-video diffusion using only a simple segmentation mask + text prompt, avoiding the need for dense motion/structural conditioning that prior controllable video generation methods require.

Technically sound and well-designed cross-attention alignment loss tied to a special [TGT] token, with a careful empirical study (Fig. 5, Table 2/3) identifying which transformer blocks and attention regions (V2T cross-attention) are most beneficial for supervision, rather than applying the loss naively everywhere.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation: a custom benchmark with a contact-based automatic metric, VBench-style video-quality decomposition, and two independent human studies (absolute evaluation and pairwise preference), all showing consistent improvements over multiple baselines (base model, fine-tuned-with-data ablation, and an adapted attention-modulation baseline).

Good range of qualitative demonstrations covering challenging cases: multiple same-type objects, non-human actors, and simultaneous actor+target control with two mask tokens, which convincingly show generalization of the mask-token mechanism.

Two well-developed downstream applications (3D-aware video content creation pipeline and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis via imitation learning) illustrate practical significance beyond pure video generation quality, connecting the work to robotics/embodied AI use cases.

Thorough ablations (block selection strategy, attention-region choice, loss weight) and a substantial supplementary section with implementation details, dataset construction, and additional qualitative comparisons support reproducibility and give confidence in the design choices.
weaknesses: The quantitative benchmark is fairly small (50 images x 5 generations per method), which combined with automatic contact-detection metrics (fixed thresholds, spatial contact only) may not robustly capture semantic correctness of the interaction (i.e., whether the actor performs the *specified action* correctly, not just makes contact).

Baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow: aside from the base CogVideoX and an adapted attention-modulation method, there is no comparison against other recent mask- or region-conditioned video generation/editing approaches, leaving the relative novelty versus closely related mask-guided methods less clearly established.

Some video-quality metrics (e.g., dynamic degree, motion smoothness) are lower for the proposed method than for the vanilla base model in Table 1, and this trade-off is not deeply analyzed or discussed, raising questions about whether the improved targeting comes at some cost to natural motion.

The zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis application requires manual scale/alignment of the imitation-learning outputs with the 3D scene (acknowledged as future work), which weakens the "zero-shot" framing and suggests the pipeline is not yet fully automatic.

The dataset curation approach uses a generic prepended sentence ("The person interacts with [TGT] object") rather than fine-grained per-instance localized descriptions, since existing captioners cannot reliably reference the target; this heuristic could limit the richness/precision of the learned target-token association and is not deeply analyzed for its impact.

The paper's own limitations section notes reliance on the visual quality of the open-source base video diffusion model and a static-camera constraint in the training data, restricting applicability to more dynamic or higher-fidelity generation settings.

strengths: The core idea—augmenting a base image-to-video diffusion model with a segmentation mask plus a dedicated [TGT] token trained with a cross-attention alignment loss—is simple, clearly motivated, and cleanly integrated into an existing MM-DiT architecture (CogVideoX) via LoRA.

The selective application of the cross-attention loss (identifying the most informative transformer blocks and choosing V2T over T2V cross-attention regions) is investigated with reasonable ablations (Tables 2-4) that at least partially justify the design choices.

The paper curates a dataset from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D tailored to the target-awareness task, and provides qualitative examples across a fairly wide range of scenarios (multiple objects of the same type, non-human agents, multi-entity source/target control).

Two downstream applications (video content creation, zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis) illustrate potential practical use cases and give the paper some breadth beyond a pure video-generation benchmark.
Reasonably extensive experimental section including automatic contact-based metrics, VBench quality metrics, and two types of human studies.
weaknesses: The evaluation benchmark is very small (50 images, 5 generated videos each) and the baselines are narrow: only the same base model (CogVideoX), a version fine-tuned on the same curated data, and a single training-free attention-modulation adaptation. No comparison to other structural/motion-conditioned controllable video methods (e.g., ControlNet-style depth/edge conditioning, other mask/box-conditioned T2V models) is provided quantitatively, which makes it hard to assess how the method stacks up against the broader controllable-video-generation literature rather than just against ablated versions of the authors' own base model.

The automatic "Contact Score" metric is coarse — any single frame with overlapping detected hand-object contact and the target mask counts as a success — which may not reliably capture whether the interaction is semantically or physically correct (e.g., accidental overlaps, wrong action type still being 'contact').

Table 1's User Pref. column reporting "(100%-above)" for the proposed method is unusual/opaque and not clearly explained; it raises questions about how preference was aggregated across the three pairwise comparisons and undermines confidence in this reported number.

The downstream applications (3D human insertion, depth-based scene composition, physics-based imitation learning) rely on a chain of off-the-shelf tools (segmentation, monocular depth, 3D pose estimation, RANSAC ground-plane fitting, manual scale alignment) with several manual/heuristic steps (e.g., "manually aligned with the 3D scene" in imitation learning outputs), making these demonstrations feel more like proof-of-concept pipelines than rigorously validated systems; no quantitative evaluation is given for either application.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: mask conditioning via channel concatenation follows InstructPix2Pix-style extension, and cross-attention alignment losses for spatial grounding are a well-established idea (e.g., prompt-to-prompt, GLIGEN-like layout control) adapted here to video transformers; the paper's contribution is largely an engineering combination and empirical tuning (selective blocks/regions) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The training data is limited to human-object interactions with a largely static camera and single-image-conditioned setups; the paper explicitly acknowledges the fixed-camera limitation and dependence on the quality of the open-source base video model, both of which constrain generality and practical impact.

Ablation in Table 4 shows that λ=1.0 slightly outperforms the chosen λ=0.1 in contact score, yet λ=0.1 is adopted without a fully convincing justification (video quality trade-off is used, but the delta is small and not statistically contextualized).

The human studies are modest in scale (50 participants, 10 videos/questions per method) and the paper does not report inter-rater agreement, variance, or statistical significance for the reported preference numbers.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practical gap: enabling precise actor-target interaction in image-to-video diffusion using only a lightweight segmentation mask cue, avoiding the need for dense motion/structural conditioning that is hard to obtain for novel HOI scenarios.

The proposed cross-attention alignment loss with a special [TGT] token is a simple, well-motivated mechanism, and the selective application to specific transformer blocks and V2T attention regions (rather than all blocks/regions) is empirically justified with clear ablations (Tables 2-4) showing why these choices matter.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation including a custom Contact Score metric, VBench-style video quality metrics, and two types of user studies (direct evaluation and A/B preference), plus qualitative comparisons against a relevant range of baselines (base I2V model, fine-tuned baseline, attention modulation, drag-based methods).

The two downstream applications (video content creation via 3D-aware human insertion + interpolation, and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis via imitation learning) demonstrate practical utility beyond the core method and go beyond a typical single-task paper.

Good generalization demonstrations: multiple objects of the same type, non-human interactions (animals), complex/small-target scenes, and extension to dual-token (actor+target) control, suggesting the method is reasonably robust and not narrowly overfit.

Thorough appendix with implementation details, dataset construction details, and a discussion of why attention modulation (a natural training-free alternative) fails, strengthening the technical soundness argument.
weaknesses: The method builds fairly incrementally on existing components (CogVideoX base model, LoRA fine-tuning, cross-attention alignment losses/prompt-to-prompt-style attention control, InstructPix2Pix-style channel extension), so the core technical novelty is more about clever combination/application than fundamentally new ideas.

The curated training dataset (1290 clips from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D) and the 50-image evaluation benchmark are relatively small scale; generalization to a broader diversity of real-world scenes, objects, and actions beyond these curated sources is not extensively probed.

Comparisons to baselines are somewhat limited since no other method directly targets this exact mask+text conditioning setting; the paper acknowledges this and constructs its own baselines (fine-tuned CogVideoX, adapted attention modulation), which, while reasonable, could be seen as less rigorous than comparing to established prior work with matched conditioning capability.

Reliance on an off-the-shelf contact detector for the primary Contact Score metric introduces potential noise/bias into the main quantitative claims, and details on detector reliability/failure modes are only briefly discussed in the appendix.

The zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis application requires substantial additional pipeline components (3D pose estimation, physics-based imitation learning, manual scale alignment as noted in the appendix), and results are shown mostly qualitatively without strong quantitative validation of physical plausibility or task success.

Limitations around video quality being bounded by the base open-source model, fixed camera trajectories, and lack of dynamic camera support are acknowledged but not addressed, somewhat narrowing the immediate applicability of the method.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel task formulation—target-aware video generation—where actor-target interactions are specified via a segmentation mask and text, filling a clear gap between fully unconstrained I2V generation and heavily-conditioned trajectory/motion-guided methods.

The proposed cross-attention alignment loss on a special [TGT] token is simple, technically sound, and clearly motivated by an analysis of MM-DiT attention regions (V2T vs T2V) and transformer block semantics; the selective application strategy is empirically justified via a systematic block-selection procedure.

Extensive and convincing experimental validation: new benchmark with 80 scenes, a Contact Score metric plus stricter variants (Contact Score@k, Interaction Score) using off-the-shelf contact/tracking detectors, two types of human studies (accuracy judgment and pairwise preference) with clear large margins over baselines, and thorough ablations (loss weight, block selection, attention region choice, mask quality/shape robustness).

Strong generalization results beyond the training distribution: non-human agents (animals, robots, cartoon characters), outdoor scenes, complex multi-object scenes, egocentric views, and multi-entity control (source+target masks) — demonstrating the method leverages base model priors rather than overfitting to the curated dataset.

Practical downstream demonstrations (zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis via imitation learning, and long-term video content creation via 3D-aware human insertion + interpolation) go beyond generation quality to show usefulness for robotics/graphics pipelines.

Very thorough appendix with implementation details, additional qualitative comparisons, discussion of failure cases (multi-object-per-mask, temporal target switching), and honest limitation discussion, which strengthens reproducibility and scientific transparency.

Comparisons against reasonably chosen baselines (vanilla CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on same data to isolate data effect, and an adapted attention-modulation baseline) isolate the contribution of the proposed loss versus additional data or naive attention control.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (cross-attention alignment loss between a special token and a spatial mask) is conceptually similar to existing attention-based grounding/editing techniques (e.g., Prompt-to-Prompt, attention modulation methods, box-constrained diffusion in T2I), so the novelty is somewhat incremental, mainly in adapting/selectively applying such losses to video diffusion transformers and pairing with a mask-conditioned architecture.

The Contact Score metric, while reasonable, is a coarse binary/frame-overlap proxy relying on an off-the-shelf hand-contact detector that is acknowledged to be unreliable for non-human agents; the primary quantitative claims rest heavily on this imperfect automatic metric plus modest-scale human studies (50 participants, 10 videos per method), which limits statistical robustness of the main results.

The training dataset is relatively small (1290 clips from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D, mostly indoor/human-centric static-camera videos), and the model exhibits known limitations (fixed camera, single object per mask, no temporal target switching) that reduce the scope of applicability compared to the broad claims made in the introduction about general "motion planning" for robotics/agents.

The two downstream applications (3D HOI imitation learning and long-term video content creation) are demonstrated only qualitatively with a handful of examples, without quantitative evaluation of physical plausibility, task success rates, or comparison to alternative pipelines, making it hard to assess how well the target-aware model actually benefits these applications versus being an illustrative proof-of-concept.

The paper does not benchmark against other recent trajectory- or drag-based methods beyond DragDiffusion and Go-with-the-Flow in a fairly limited qualitative comparison (Fig. 4); a more systematic quantitative comparison against these or other structure-guided baselines (depth/edge conditioning) would strengthen claims of superiority.

Some architectural choices (e.g., extra channel per target mask, single fixed target per video) are acknowledged as scalability limitations but not addressed even preliminarily, leaving open how the method would extend to more complex multi-target or temporally varying interaction scenarios central to the paper's stated long-term vision.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and relatively underexplored problem: giving image-to-video diffusion models explicit 'target awareness' via a segmentation mask plus a special [TGT] token, which is a clean and simple mechanism.

The proposed selective cross-attention loss (restricted to V2T attention and to a semantically-identified subset of transformer blocks) is a reasonable and empirically-justified design choice, backed by a fairly thorough set of ablations (Tables 2-6) on block selection, attention region, loss weight, and mask quality/shape robustness.

The paper provides extensive qualitative evidence of generalization beyond the training distribution (non-human agents, outdoor scenes, complex multi-object scenes, egocentric views, multiple objects of the same category), which is a genuinely interesting emergent property of leveraging a pretrained backbone.

Two downstream applications (zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis via imitation learning, and long-form video content creation via 3D human insertion + interpolation) demonstrate practical utility beyond the core generation task.

The appendix is unusually thorough: automatic mask acquisition pipeline, robustness to noisy captions/prompts, extended targeting metrics (Contact Score k-frame variants, Interaction Score using point tracking), attention-mechanism analysis, and an honest limitations section with several documented failure cases (multi-object masks, temporal target switching).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it is essentially a LoRA fine-tune of an existing SOTA I2V model (CogVideoX) with an added mask input channel and a cross-attention alignment loss borrowed from prior prompt-to-prompt/attention-control literature (Hertz et al., 2022); the novelty is largely in the specific application/combination rather than a new modeling principle.

The evaluation benchmark is small and self-constructed (only 80 test images, 400 generated videos), and the primary metric (Contact Score) relies on an off-the-shelf hand-contact detector not designed for this task, whose reliability for the claimed accuracy gains is not independently validated; the paper itself notes in the appendix that this detector fails for non-human agents, undermining quantitative support for the generalization claims that are only shown qualitatively.

Baselines for quantitative comparison are limited to three CogVideoX-based variants and one attention-modulation baseline; no comparison is made against other trajectory/structure-conditioned controllable video generation methods (depth, motion, drag-based) in the main quantitative table, only qualitatively for two drag-based methods, making the strength of the claimed improvement hard to fully contextualize.

Video generation quality (VBench metrics) is essentially on par with baselines rather than improved, so the gains are confined to the newly introduced, self-defined target-alignment metric — raising concerns about whether the improvement generalizes to standard quality/fidelity notions used elsewhere in the field.

Training data scale is modest (1290 curated clips from two existing datasets, BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D), and the method depends on noisy auto-generated captions combined with a fixed template sentence, an ad hoc workaround (Sec 4.4) whose robustness is only partially explored (Table 8).

The framework has notable structural limitations acknowledged by the authors (single fixed target per video, no multi-object-per-mask support, extra input channel per target limiting scalability, static camera bias in training data), several of which constrain real-world applicability and are left entirely as future work.

User studies, while included, use small crowdsourced samples (50 participants, 10 videos per method) and binary/forced-choice judgments, which is a relatively weak protocol for establishing significance of the reported large margins.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and practically useful new task formulation — target-aware video diffusion that lets an actor interact with a user-specified object (via mask) while following a text-described action — bridging video generation with motion planning/robotics.

The proposed method is simple and elegant: extending an I2V backbone with a mask channel plus a special [TGT] token whose cross-attention is explicitly aligned to the target mask via an auxiliary loss, applied selectively to the most semantically informative transformer blocks and cross-attention regions (V2T).

Extensive and well-designed ablations justify each design choice: selection of transformer blocks, choice of cross-attention region (V2T vs T2V vs both), loss weight, robustness to mask shape/quality (dilation/erosion, circular masks), and automatic mask generation pipeline.

Comprehensive evaluation combining a new Contact Score metric (plus stricter k-frame and Interaction Score variants), VBench quality metrics, and two independent human user studies, all consistently favoring the proposed method over reasonable baselines (vanilla CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, and an attention-modulation baseline).

Strong demonstrated generalization beyond the training distribution: non-human agents (animals, robots, cartoon characters), outdoor scenes, egocentric views, complex multi-object scenes, and scenes with multiple same-category objects — despite training only on indoor human-object interaction clips.

Two concrete downstream applications (zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis with physics-based imitation learning, and long-term video content creation via 3D-aware human insertion + interpolation) that showcase broader significance beyond the core generation task.

Thorough, honest appendix with implementation details (LoRA config, compute cost, inference time), additional robustness analyses (noisy captions, perturbed prompts), attention-mechanism analysis, and a candid discussion of limitations/failure cases (multi-object-per-mask, temporal target switching, contact-detector limitations for non-human agents).
weaknesses: The benchmark used for the main quantitative comparison is relatively small (80 images, 400 generated videos), which is modest for establishing a new task/benchmark, though appendix experiments add some additional robustness checks.

The core technical contribution (a special token + cross-attention alignment loss for spatial grounding) is conceptually close to existing cross-attention-based layout/grounding control methods (e.g., prompt-to-prompt style approaches); novelty lies more in careful application/adaptation to video target-awareness and selective block/region tuning than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

The architecture requires an additional input channel per specified target and assumes a single fixed target mask for the whole clip, limiting scalability to many targets and preventing temporal target switching (acknowledged as future work).

The Contact Score metric depends on an off-the-shelf hand-contact detector that is human-centric, making it unreliable/inapplicable for the non-human-agent generalization results, which are therefore only qualitatively validated.

Downstream applications (3D HOI motion synthesis, long-term video creation) are demonstrated mainly qualitatively without rigorous quantitative evaluation of their own (e.g., physical plausibility metrics, task success rates), so their practical significance is not fully substantiated.

Training data and evaluation rely on specific static-camera indoor datasets (BEHAVE, Ego-Exo4D subset), and the model inherits fixed-camera bias; broader camera dynamics and larger-scale/more diverse interaction datasets are left to future work.
